name: Adam Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Castle Road Garage, an independent place near the football ground, three bays and Ray, the owner, who's been fixing cars for thirty years. I do services, brakes, cambelts with Ray watching, and I'm still slower than I'd like on anything with a lot of trim to take off. I use AI every day, I photograph a fault code, ask it for likely causes and the repair steps, and then Ray tells me which one he'd bet on. I like the puzzle, and I like that the customer pays for a result, not for hours sitting at a desk.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, I rent a flat above a barber's, and I've got about three months of costs saved plus an old hatchback I'm fixing up to sell. I buy a cheap car every couple of months, fix it in Ray's yard on Sundays and sell it online, maybe three hundred profit each time. My dad drove a taxi for twenty-five years, and he's always said, work for yourself if you can. That's the plan, my own garage one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the AI tools are great and anybody who isn't using them is missing out, hype or not. At the garage I'd keep showing Ray the shortcuts. Online I'd post the cars I flip, that's my real marketing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, actually good. I keep my edge with the tools, the garage stays busy and I keep flipping cars. If AI stays a handy tool, I'll have my own garage by thirty-five with a phone that thinks faster than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working for Ray, keep flipping a car every two months and put the profit straight into savings. I'd do the hybrid course next spring. I'd start looking at small units to rent in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit impatient to get going on my own. Every Sunday in the yard feels like practice for my own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you outside of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's up and I'd like to buy one day, but I've got the side money. My mum worries more than I do. She keeps asking when I'll settle down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ray think of your car flipping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He grumbles about his yard, then gives me tips. I think he likes it, he started the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best time to be young and willing to learn. I'd tell my friends to use the tools or get left behind. Online I'd share how I use AI at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a big chance for me, because I already use it. Ray might lean on me more for diagnostics, and AI does the paperwork. A small garage with good AI can quote, order and book like a dealership, and that's my way in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up AI booking and quoting for Ray in the first months and ask for more responsibility. I'd keep flipping cars and maybe rent a small unit for weekend jobs within a year. I'd keep saving and avoid any debt until it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. It feels like the door's opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big dealerships with big front desks, maybe, and people who refuse to learn. That's harsh, but that's the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ray say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, then let me do it. He's not daft, he knows it saves him time.

I'd tell friends to **use the tools** or get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and people need to move fast, and that the government shouldn't get in the way. I'd tell my friends to learn whatever robots can't do. Online I'd share what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my edge disappears in 2028, everyone has the same AI. By 2031 robots fix cars, and my garage plan looks shaky. I spent years planning my own garage, and two years later the robots could open one next door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep flipping cars hard and save everything, while there's still money in it. I'd look at owning robots instead of competing with them, maybe a small robot repair business. I'd move back with my parents if needed to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be busy. Busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still open your own garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but a different kind, one that owns the robots. That needs money I don't have yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work for yourself, same as always. He'd also say, come home and save. I'd probably listen.

do: Flip cars hard and **save everything** while it lasts.

S2.quote: I spent years planning my own garage, and two years later the robots could open one next door.
fieldNote: His **garage dream** suddenly looks shaky once robots arrive in 2031.
He'd rather **own the robots** than compete with them, but lacks the money.
He'd accept **family support** from his parents without embarrassment.

steps.text: Flip cars faster and save every profit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get ahead if people hustle. I'd talk up apprenticeships and small businesses. I'd share tips online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to open a small garage and plan for robots. Five years is enough to open my own garage and decide whether the robots work for me or against me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rent a unit in year two and keep flipping cars. I'd save for robot kit when it arrives. I'd keep using AI to run the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, because the timing has to be right. But I like a challenge, and this is the biggest one going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Opening too late, or too early, and getting stuck with debt. I'd need to watch the market closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still work for Ray?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year or two, part-time, while I build my own place. Ray would understand, he did the same thing at my age.

I'd talk up **apprenticeships** and small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a great runway for anyone willing to work. I'd tell young people to learn trades and start businesses. I'd share my story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd have my own garage and be ready to buy robots. With ten years warning, the robots stop being a threat and start being my best employees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open my garage in a few years, build customers and save for robots. I'd keep using AI tools daily. I'd think about settling down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. It's the picture I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would settling down look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marriage, kids, a house near my parents. My mum would be thrilled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you're wrong about owning robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd sell up and do something else. That's business.

S4.quote: With ten years warning, the robots stop being a threat and start being my best employees.
fieldNote: He sees robots as **assets to own**, not rivals for his job.
He'd **settle down** near his parents with a decade's warning.
He accepts **business risk** as normal and would sell up if wrong.

steps.text: Open his own garage within a few years
Buy workshop robots when they arrive

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit before I've built my garage. What would help is low rents for small businesses and fewer rules on starting up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about owning things. Most people ask if they'll lose their job, but I want to know if I'll own the robot that took it.

headlineQuote: Most people ask if they'll lose their job, but I want to know if I'll own the robot that took it.
portrait: Adam is a **junior mechanic** at an independent garage who uses AI every day.
He **flips used cars** on Sundays for extra income.
He's single, with about **three months** saved, and plans his own garage.
He sees AI as **opportunity**, but fast AGI shakes his plans.
With time, he plans to **own robots** rather than compete with them.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, before he's built his own garage.
whatWouldHelp: **Low rents** for small businesses and **fewer rules** on starting up.
